You express regret and reproach with the past conditional: j’aurais dû, tu aurais pu, il aurait fallu, j’aurais aimé, si seulement…
to get (something) wrong, to mix up
I should have learned Spanish earlier.
You should have taken the ring.
I would have liked to see Seville.
To form the past conditional: avoir / être in the conditional + past participle.
To express regret: j’aurais dû, j’aurais pu, j’aurais aimé.
To make a reproach: tu aurais pu…, vous auriez dû…, il aurait fallu…
To use "si seulement" + pluperfect for an impossible wish.
To tell the story of something that didn’t go to plan and comment on it.
Sunday, 1 April, Easter Sunday, eleven at night. Radu calls Ioana from Seville, after asking Lucia to marry him. Nothing went as he had planned.
Radu! So? Did she say yes? Tell me!
She said yes. But Ioana, it was a disaster. I should have listened to you. I should have learned Spanish properly.
This morning I went to see the grandfather to ask his permission. I’d rehearsed my sentence a hundred times. And I got one word wrong.
Instead of saying "I want to marry your granddaughter", I said "I want to marry your wife". "Su mujer" instead of "su nieta". In front of the grandmother.
(bursts out laughing) No! And what did he do?
He looked at me for a minute without saying anything. I could have sunk through the floor. Then the grandmother answered that she was flattered, but already taken.
You could have asked me to check your sentence! I speak a bit of Spanish, you know.
I know. I should have shown it to you. But wait, it’s not over. In the evening I forgot the ring at the hotel.
I was in the courtyard, under the orange tree, on my knees in front of Lucia, while the procession went by in the street. And I put my hand in my pocket. Empty.
I told the truth. Lucia laughed for five minutes. Then she said: "You should have seen your face. Yes, silly. Yes, even without a ring."
(moved) You see? It all turned out well. If only Hélène could have heard this story…
She will. I’ll tell her myself, on Wednesday. With the ring, this time.

The past conditional is formed with avoir or être in the PRESENT CONDITIONAL + past participle (like the passé composé, but with the auxiliary in the conditional):
You already saw it in ch. 35, in type 3 "si" sentences: "Si j’avais su, je serais venu." Here we use it on its own, for regrets and reproaches.
2. Regret: j’aurais dû, j’aurais pu, j’aurais aimé
I didn’t, and I regret it
I could have sunk through the floor.
The typical mistake: "Je devais apprendre l’espagnol" (imperfect) means "I was supposed to learn" (it was the plan); it doesn’t express regret. For regret: "J’AURAIS DÛ apprendre".
In the second and third person, the same forms become REPROACHES:
You could have asked me to check your sentence!
You should have shown it to me.
You should have seen your face! (joke)
"Il aurait fallu" is impersonal: + infinitive (general) or + que + subjunctive (for someone): "Il aurait fallu que je te la montre."
"Si seulement" (if only) expresses a strong wish. For the PAST (impossible to change), it is followed by the PLUPERFECT; for the PRESENT, by the IMPERFECT:
Si seulement j’avais plus de temps !
If only I had more time!
Si seulement Hélène avait pu entendre…
5. Other uses of the past conditional
In the press, the past conditional expresses UNCONFIRMED information (like English "reportedly"):
The thief reportedly left through the window. (not certain)
The accident reportedly left three people injured.
Romanian has exactly the same construction ("ar fi plecat"), so it’s easy to understand. Just watch the participle agreement with "être".
She would have come with us.
"The thief reportedly left through the window." (press)

If only Hélène could have heard this story…

On Thursday 29 March, Radu and Lucia flew to Seville. Throughout the flight, Radu practised his Spanish sentences, eyes closed, moving his lips. Lucia pretended to read a magazine. In reality she was watching him out of the corner of her eye, and found it very hard not to laugh.

Lucia’s family house was in the Triana district, on the other side of the river. It was an old white house with green shutters and, in the middle, a courtyard tiled in blue, where a hundred-year-old orange tree grew. It was covered in white blossom, and the whole courtyard smelled of the sweet scent of orange flowers.

The whole family was waiting for them in the courtyard. Lucia’s parents, her two aunts, about ten cousins and, seated in a large wicker armchair, the grandfather, don Manuel. A lean, upright old man, with white hair combed back and a guitarist’s hands, long and slender. He didn’t smile.

Next to him stood the grandmother, doña Carmen, small, plump and smiling, in a flowery apron. She hugged Radu as if she had known him all her life and began to talk to him very fast, in Spanish, pinching his cheeks. Radu understood only one word in ten.

It was Holy Week. The whole city was out in the streets. In the evenings, the processions went slowly by, with their statues carried on huge platforms covered in flowers and candles, to the sound of drums and trumpets. Radu had never seen anything like it. He watched it all open-mouthed, like a child.

He had planned to propose on Easter Sunday. But first he had to ask the grandfather’s permission. Ioana had advised him to, and Lucia, without knowing what it was about, had once told him that in her family nothing important was done without don Manuel’s approval.

On Sunday morning, Radu got up at six. He put on his white shirt, rehearsed his sentence in front of the mirror twenty times, then went down into the courtyard. Don Manuel was already there, in his armchair, with his guitar on his knees, and doña Carmen was watering the plants. Radu took a deep breath.

"Señor," he began, in a trembling voice. "Quiero casarme con su mujer." There was absolute silence. Doña Carmen dropped her watering can. Don Manuel slowly raised his eyes from his guitar and looked at Radu for a long time without saying anything. Radu felt that something was wrong, but he didn’t know what.

Then doña Carmen burst out laughing. An enormous laugh that echoed around the whole courtyard and brought half the family out of their rooms in their pyjamas. She was laughing so hard she had to sit down on the edge of the fountain. Between two bursts of laughter, she said something in Spanish, pointing to her wedding ring.

A cousin who spoke a little French translated, trying to keep a straight face: "She says she’s very flattered, but she’s already been married for fifty-five years. You said ’su mujer’, his wife. Not ’su nieta’, his granddaughter." Radu went as red as a tomato. He would have liked to disappear under the blue tiles of the courtyard.

Don Manuel still hadn’t smiled. He put down his guitar, stood up, came over to Radu and looked him straight in the eye. Radu thought: "I should have asked Ioana to check my sentence. I should have stayed in Lyon. I should have chosen a fiancée whose grandfather doesn’t play the guitar."

The old man put a hand on his shoulder and said something slowly, articulating each word so that Radu would understand. The cousin translated: "He says: I know what you meant. Tonight. Under the orange tree. And he also says that if you make his granddaughter cry, he’ll throw you into the Guadalquivir."

All day long, Radu acted as if nothing had happened. He went with the family to Mass, he ate torrijas, he watched one last procession. Lucia found him strange, nervous, distracted. She asked him several times whether everything was all right. Each time he answered: "Muy bien", with a slightly too broad smile.

In the evening, when night had fallen, the family discreetly withdrew into the house. Only a few lanterns lit the courtyard. In the street you could hear the last procession of Holy Week going by, with its distant drums. Radu asked Lucia to come and sit with him under the orange tree.

He knelt down in front of her on the blue tiles. Lucia raised her hands to her mouth. He began his speech, in French this time, the one he had been preparing for six weeks. Then he put his hand in his jacket pocket to take out the little blue velvet box. The pocket was empty.

He checked the other pocket. Empty too. Then his trouser pockets. Nothing. And he remembered: the box had been left on the bedside table at the hotel, where he had put it that morning so as not to lose it during the procession. He wanted to shout. He wanted to cry. He stayed on his knees, empty-handed.

"Lucia," he said at last, in a very small voice. "I had a ring. It belonged to my great-grandmother. It’s very beautiful. And it’s at the hotel. On the bedside table. I’m an idiot. But I’d still like to ask you if you’ll marry me." There was a long silence.

Then Lucia burst out laughing. Exactly like her grandmother that morning. A laugh that made the orange blossoms tremble. She laughed for a good five minutes, doubled over, wiping her tears. Radu, still on his knees, didn’t know whether to laugh with her or run off towards the Guadalquivir.

At last she calmed down. She knelt down facing him, took his face in her hands and said: "You should have seen your face. Yes, silly. Yes, even without a ring. Yes, even if you ask for my grandmother’s hand." And she kissed him, under the orange tree, to the sound of the drums.

At that very moment, all the windows of the house opened. The whole family had been watching from the start, hidden behind the curtains. There were shouts, applause, cries of bravo. Doña Carmen was crying with joy. And don Manuel, standing at his window, was finally smiling. For the first time since Radu’s arrival.

The old man came down into the courtyard with his guitar. He sat down under the orange tree, tuned his instrument and played. A slow, deep flamenco that spoke of love and of the night. Lucia stood up and danced for Radu, as she had danced one September evening in the student residence, the night they met.

Around eleven, Radu finally plucked up the courage to call his sister. He told her everything: the "su mujer", the empty pocket, Lucia’s laughter. Ioana was laughing so hard at the other end of the line that she woke Rose-Hélène. Then Radu called Iași. His mother cried. His father said: "At last." And the grandmother asked when the wedding would be.

That night, Radu hardly slept. He kept going over all his mistakes of the day. He could have practised his Spanish better. He should have checked his pockets. Perhaps he should have chosen a less complicated day than Easter Sunday. But every time he looked at Lucia, asleep beside him with a smile, he told himself he regretted absolutely nothing.

The next morning, before leaving, Radu went back to the hotel for the ring. He put it on Lucia’s finger in the courtyard, in front of the whole family, under the orange tree, taking great care not to get the wrong finger. Doña Carmen checked for herself. Don Manuel nodded, satisfied.

The following Wednesday, back in Lyon, Radu and Lucia went up to Fourvière with Julien. Hélène was in bed. She hardly got up any more. But when she saw them come in, her face lit up. She asked Madame Lambert to help her sit up, and she wanted to know everything.

Radu told his story for the third time. He told it better than the other times, with gestures, voices, doña Carmen’s watering can and don Manuel’s terrible stare. Hélène laughed so hard she had to catch her breath several times. Madame Lambert, in the corridor, was laughing too, pretending not to listen.

Then Hélène asked to see the ring. Lucia held out her hand. Hélène looked at it through her magnifying glass for a long time. A small red stone on a worn silver band. "It has been worn by many happy women," she said. "You can tell. Rings keep the happiness of those who have worn them."

She looked out of the window, to the south, as if she could see Spain beyond the rooftops. "I would have liked to see Seville," she murmured. "Henri wanted to take me there for my twenty-first birthday. He said there were orange trees in every street. We never went."

Lucia rummaged in her bag. She took out a small sprig of orange blossom, its white flowers slightly wilted, wrapped in a damp handkerchief. "I picked it in my grandfather’s courtyard on Sunday morning," she said. "For you. I knew you’d want to smell Seville."

Hélène took the sprig in her trembling hands. She raised it to her face and breathed in the scent, eyes closed, for a very long time. Nobody said anything. Then she smiled, and two tears ran down her cheeks. "There," she said softly. "Now I’ve seen Seville."

Before they left, she beckoned Radu over. "Monday is the 15th of April," she said. "The foundation stone. I’ll be there. The doctor can say what he likes. I have to see the room begin." Radu wanted to protest, but Julien signalled to him to keep quiet. There was no arguing with Hélène.

On the way out, Julien saw the little sprig of orange blossom on the bedside table, in a glass of water, next to the 1962 photo and the score of the waltz. Hélène had already fallen asleep, a smile on her lips, and the sweet scent of the flowers of Seville hung throughout the room.

After Radu leaves, Lucia’s grandfather, don Manuel, sends him a letter (translated by Lucia). Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end you answer 4 questions.
Dear Radu, my granddaughter helped me write this letter in French. I would have liked to write it myself, but at eighty-four you don’t learn a language in six weeks. You, on the other hand, tried.
When you asked me for my wife’s hand, I could have got angry. My Carmen, though, laughed all day. She says that in fifty-five years of marriage, nobody had ever paid her such a lovely compliment.
I must confess something to you. I too botched my proposal. In 1973 I had prepared a song for Carmen. I should have tuned my guitar first: it was completely out of tune.
If only you had seen her face! She laughed, exactly like Lucia the other evening. And she said yes. The women of this family like men who make mistakes sincerely.

You could have given up after your first mistake. You didn’t. You came back in the evening, you knelt under my orange tree, without a ring, and you told the truth. That is why I give you my granddaughter.

One last thing: you should have stayed longer. Come back this summer. I’ll teach you three guitar chords. And Carmen will teach you the difference between "mujer" and "nieta". Your future grandfather, Manuel.
